newsitem.title: USA: Republicans protest Democrat campaign ads.
newsitem.headline: Republicans protest Democrat campaign ads.

text.p: Senate Republicans on Wednesday accused Democrats and labour unions of massive campaign finance law violations in their television political commercials.

The National Republican Senatorial Committee said in a complaint to the Federal Election Commission that its Democratic counterpart and the AFL-CIO were running "issue" commercials attacking Republican Senate candidates paid for by labour unions and special interest groups.

The Republicans said issue ads were not supposed to be shown when Congress was out of session or to support or oppose the election of a candidate. They said the ads were used in coordination with other commercials on behalf of Democratic candidates.

"The massive statutory violations currently being undertaken by the Democratic National Committee, Democratic Senate Campaign Committee, AFL-CIO and the various Democratic state party committees with respect to this so-called issue advertising are so outrageous and unconscionable that it is the constitutional duty of the commission to act without delay to investigate these allegations and stop this wholesale circumvention of federal law," the complaint said.

The Republicans said the ads all had the same themes in accusing Senate Republican candidates of voting to cut Social Security or Medicare or to give tax breaks to the wealthy. They asked the FEC to order the commercials withdrawn and to penalise the Democrats and the union federation.
The Republicans also sent letters to television stations across the country asking them not to run the ads.

Two weeks ago, House Republicans filed suit in federal court seeking to force the Federal Election Commission to act on its charges that the AFL-CIO had illegally spent millions of dollars to aid Democrats.

The AFL-CIO has committed $35 million to television advertising mainly targeted at the districts of vulnerable Republicans. The union group said its advertising was designed to highlight issues, not political candidates, and was free speech protected by the Constitution.
The National Republican Congressional Committee, which helps Republican House candidates, Wednesday began to run an ad accusing the AFL-CIO of trying to buy control of Congress.
